runs.output:
Internal engineering memo: local AI hardware versus better utilisation

To: platform, ML, and infrastructure leads
From: engineering leadership
Date: current planning cycle
Re: whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

The decision is not simply “buy more” or “do nothing.” It is whether the next dollar should expand capacity or reduce waste. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, instrument the workload honestly, and only then approve a bounded hardware purchase. Do not sign a large multi-year commitment yet. Buy enough to remove a proven bottleneck, keep cloud burst as a pressure valve, and revisit after two quarters of measured demand.

The cost case is easy to misread. Local hardware has a visible price tag, but the real cost includes power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, staff time, and the opportunity cost of engineers spending weeks on provisioning instead of product work. A GPU that sits idle for most of the day is not cheap; it is expensive idle capacity. Conversely, a modest purchase can be justified if it removes a recurring queue, protects latency-sensitive workloads, or avoids repeated cloud overruns. The right question is not “what does the machine cost?” but “what does the workload cost per useful inference, per second of latency, and per incident?”

Latency deserves separate treatment. Local deployment can reduce network dependence and keep sensitive data inside our boundary, which may matter for some workloads. But latency is not improved by owning more accelerators if requests are still serialised, batched poorly, or routed through a slow control plane. Interactive features need predictable tail latency, not just average throughput. Batch jobs need throughput and cost efficiency. These are different operating points. If our current bottleneck is scheduling, queueing, model loading, or data movement, more hardware will mostly add idle capacity. If the bottleneck is genuinely compute saturation during predictable peaks, then additional capacity becomes rational.

Reliability is another reason to be cautious. Local systems concentrate risk: a failed node, a cooling event, a driver regression, or a single rack can affect many services. That can be acceptable for internal batch workloads, but less acceptable for customer-facing paths unless we add redundancy, health checks, failover, and clear ownership. Cloud services offer elasticity and operational maturity, but they introduce network variance, vendor dependence, and variable spend. The best answer is often hybrid: local for predictable, sensitive, or latency-sensitive workloads; cloud for bursty, experimental, or low-confidence demand.

Opportunity cost is the part teams underestimate. Every hour spent tuning utilisation, profiling memory use, improving batching, and cleaning up model serving is an hour not spent on features. That is a real cost, but it is also a learning investment. If we buy first and measure later, we may discover that the workload was misunderstood. If we measure first, we may find that a small set of changes—better queueing, smaller models, caching, quantization, or tighter routing—delivers most of the benefit. The memo should not pretend this is certain. Demand forecasts are uncertain, model sizes are moving quickly, and prices may shift. We should treat the plan as reversible.

Reversibility argues for staged action. Prefer leases or short-term commitments over large purchases. Keep cloud burst enabled. Design services so models can move between local and cloud without rewriting application logic. Avoid locking critical paths to one vendor or one rack. If we do buy, buy modular capacity that can be repurposed as workloads change, and avoid exotic configurations that only fit today’s assumptions.

Concretely, I recommend the following posture. First, instrument utilisation for four to six weeks: GPU time, memory, queue depth, p95 latency, failure rate, and cost per workload. Second, fix the obvious waste: idle models, oversized instances, poor batching, and duplicated pipelines. Third, run a small pilot for the highest-value workload, with a clear success threshold. Fourth, if the pilot shows sustained saturation and the cloud alternative is materially worse on latency or data control, approve a limited purchase sized to the proven gap, not the peak fantasy. Fifth, revisit after two quarters and cancel or renegotiate if utilisation remains low.

The uncertainty is real. We may be wrong about demand, and the market may change. But the cost of being wrong is asymmetric: buying too much hardware locks us into waste, while improving utilisation and buying later preserves options. The goal is not maximum local ownership. It is reliable, affordable AI capability with enough headroom to grow. Buy when the evidence is strong, keep the path reversible, and do not let a visible machine purchase substitute for understanding the workload.

To: Engineering leadership
From: Platform and infrastructure working group
Re: Local AI hardware: buy more or use what we have better

Recommendation up front: do not commit a large new hardware purchase yet. Run a focused utilisation and reliability programme for the next two quarters, instrument the workloads, and only then approve a targeted expansion. If the evidence shows sustained queueing, poor batching, or repeated latency misses that cannot be fixed by scheduling, model routing, or capacity-aware serving, buy a smaller, reversible increment rather than a fleet-wide refresh.

The central question is not whether local AI is worth doing; it is whether the next dollar should buy silicon or should buy better behaviour from the silicon we already own. Local inference is attractive because it keeps data inside our boundary, reduces dependence on external endpoints, and can improve tail latency for sensitive workloads. But those benefits are easy to overstate. A GPU that sits at 18 percent utilisation for most of the day is not a capacity asset; it is a fixed cost with a noisy workload attached. The first-order fix is to understand what the hardware is actually doing: which services call it, how often, with what prompt sizes, batching patterns, concurrency, and failure modes, and whether the bottleneck is compute, memory bandwidth, networking, storage, or simply poor admission control.

Cost should be evaluated as total cost of ownership, not sticker price. New hardware carries purchase price, power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, driver and runtime upgrades, staff time, and the risk that the workload mix changes before the asset reaches useful life. Existing hardware carries a different cost: idle capacity, duplicated experiments, and the opportunity cost of engineers spending time on manual tuning instead of product work. If we buy before we understand the gap, we may pay twice: once for the machines and again for the inefficiency that remains.

Latency deserves separate treatment from throughput. A batch job can tolerate queueing; a user-facing assistant cannot. We should separate offline evaluation, background summarisation, and interactive inference into different service classes with explicit latency budgets. Interactive traffic should be protected from batch bursts, and batch work should be allowed to fill spare capacity without starving interactive requests. This is where utilisation and latency can be reconciled: not by maximising average utilisation, but by matching each workload to the right queue, model size, and hardware class.

Reliability is the other reason to be cautious. Local systems fail in ways cloud services do not: driver mismatches, thermal throttling, memory pressure, degraded GPUs, and operator error during upgrades. More hardware increases the number of failure domains unless we also improve observability, health checks, rollback paths, and runbooks. A larger fleet without better operations can lower reliability even while raising nominal capacity. Conversely, better utilisation can reduce the number of active nodes, simplify the failure surface, and make incidents easier to diagnose.

Opportunity cost is easy to miss. Every dollar spent on hardware is a dollar not spent on evaluation, data quality, model selection, observability, or product features. If the team is spending weeks waiting for local inference to become usable, the real bottleneck may be workflow design rather than silicon. Improving utilisation also creates option value: it tells us whether the workload is genuinely growing, whether demand is seasonal, and whether a smaller model or better routing can meet the same SLO.

Reversibility matters. Software changes, scheduling policies, and routing rules are cheap to undo. Hardware purchases are not. A staged approach preserves optionality: we can test whether a modest increase in capacity, or a change in serving architecture, closes the gap. If the gap persists, the purchase is better informed and more likely to be used. If it does not, we avoid stranded assets.

Uncertainty remains. We do not yet know whether demand will grow steadily, spike seasonally, or be dominated by a few high-value workloads. We also do not know how much of the current pain comes from model choice rather than hardware. The right response is not to pretend certainty, but to make the decision reversible and evidence-driven.

Proposed path: instrument for four to six weeks, classify workloads, set latency budgets, tune batching and admission control, and review utilisation weekly. If interactive p95 latency remains above target after those changes, or if sustained utilisation exceeds roughly 70 to 80 percent with queueing, approve a limited purchase. Otherwise, defer the purchase and revisit with the next planning cycle. This is not a hedge against action; it is a disciplined way to buy the right capacity at the right time.
